topics.topic: Introduction to computers and their organization

subtopics.title: Block diagram of a computer
subtopics.theory_md:
A computer takes **input**, **processes** it under a stored **program**, keeps results in **memory** and gives **output** (von Neumann stored-program model).

- **Input unit**: keyboard, mouse, scanner.
- **Output unit**: monitor, printer.
- **CPU** = **ALU** (arithmetic and logic operations) + **CU** (control unit: fetches, decodes, directs) + **registers** (fastest small storage, e.g. PC, IR, accumulator).
- **Memory**: primary (RAM, ROM) and secondary (hard disk, SSD).

Data and instructions both sit in memory; the CPU repeats **fetch, decode, execute**.
subtopics.basics_md: A computer works like a cook. Ingredients come in (input), the cook follows a recipe held in his head (program in memory), works at the counter (ALU) while a manager gives orders (CU), and the dish goes out (output).
key_points: Five units: input, output, memory, ALU, control unit (CPU = ALU + CU + registers)
CU fetches, decodes and controls; ALU does arithmetic and logic
Program and data are stored in memory (stored-program concept)
Cycle is fetch, decode, execute

questions.q: Which part of the CPU performs arithmetic and logical operations?
questions.why: The ALU does arithmetic and logic; the CU only directs the other units.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT part of the CPU?
questions.why: The hard disk is secondary storage outside the CPU.

questions.q: Draw the block diagram of a computer in words and state the function of each block.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Block diagram:** Input unit -> [ CPU: ALU + Control unit + Registers ] <-> Memory unit -> Output unit.

1. **Input unit**: takes data and instructions from the user (keyboard, mouse) and converts them to binary.
2. **Memory unit**: stores the program, data and results (primary RAM/ROM, secondary disk).
3. **ALU**: arithmetic (+, -, *, /) and logical (AND, OR, comparison) operations.
4. **Control unit**: fetches each instruction, decodes it and sends control signals to all units.
5. **Output unit**: shows results (monitor, printer).
points: Input unit takes data and instructions
Memory stores program, data, results
ALU does arithmetic and logic
CU fetches, decodes and controls
Output unit gives results

questions.q: Differentiate between ALU and control unit.
questions.model_answer_md:
| ALU | Control unit |
|---|---|
| Performs arithmetic and logical operations | Fetches and decodes instructions and controls the sequence |
| Works on data given to it | Does not process data; sends control signals to ALU, memory, I/O |
| Result goes to a register or memory | Directs where the result goes |
points: ALU: arithmetic and logic operations
CU: fetch, decode, control signals
CU does not process data

subtopics.title: Memory, hardware and software
subtopics.theory_md:
**Memory hierarchy** (fast and small to slow and large): registers, cache, **RAM** (primary, volatile, read/write), **ROM** (non-volatile, holds boot program), secondary storage (HDD, SSD; non-volatile).

Units: 1 byte = 8 bits; 1 KB = $2^{10}$ bytes = 1024 B; 1 MB = $2^{20}$ B; 1 GB = $2^{30}$ B.

**Hardware** = physical parts. **Software** = programs: **system software** (operating system, compiler, assembler, interpreter) and **application software** (word processor, browser).

**Compiler** translates the whole program at once; **interpreter** line by line; **assembler** converts assembly to machine code.
subtopics.basics_md: Your desk is RAM: small and quick, cleared when you leave. The cupboard is the hard disk: big and slow, but things stay. Hardware is what you can kick; software is what you cannot.
key_points: RAM is volatile primary memory; ROM and disk are non-volatile
Hierarchy: register, cache, RAM, secondary (speed falls, size rises)
Hardware = physical; software = system and application
Compiler: whole program; interpreter: line by line; assembler: assembly to machine code

subtopics.title: Number systems to decimal
subtopics.theory_md:
Positional systems: **binary** base 2 (0,1), **octal** base 8 (0-7), **decimal** base 10, **hexadecimal** base 16 (0-9, A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15).

To get decimal, multiply each digit by $\text{base}^{\text{position}}$ (positions $0,1,2,\dots$ to the left of the point, $-1,-2,\dots$ to the right) and add.

Example: $(1101.101)_2 = 1\cdot2^3+1\cdot2^2+0\cdot2^1+1\cdot2^0+1\cdot2^{-1}+0\cdot2^{-2}+1\cdot2^{-3}=13.625$.

Powers of 2 to remember: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256; powers of 16: 1, 16, 256, 4096.
subtopics.basics_md: In 425 the digit 4 means four hundreds, because it sits two places from the right: $4\times10^2$. Other bases do the same with their own base.
key_points: Write each digit times base^position, then add
Hex letters: A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15
Fraction digits use negative powers
Show the expansion line and the final answer with the base subscript

subtopics.title: Decimal to binary, octal, hex and between bases
subtopics.theory_md:
**Integer part**: divide repeatedly by the base, write the remainders, read them **bottom to top**.
**Fraction part**: multiply repeatedly by the base, write the integer parts, read **top to bottom**; stop when the fraction is 0 (or at the asked number of places).

**Shortcuts**: binary to octal groups of **3 bits** from the point; binary to hex groups of **4 bits**; pad with zeros at the ends (left of the integer, right of the fraction).

$(101101110)_2 = (101\ 101\ 110)_2 = (556)_8$ and $(0001\ 0110\ 1110)_2=(16E)_{16}$.
subtopics.basics_md: Dividing by 2 asks 'is the number odd?' and keeps the answer as the last bit; halving again finds the next bit. That is why the first remainder is the last (lowest) bit and you read upwards.
key_points: Integer: repeated division, remainders read bottom to top
Fraction: repeated multiplication, integer parts read top to bottom
Binary to octal: groups of 3; to hex: groups of 4

subtopics.title: Flowchart symbols and rules
subtopics.theory_md:
A **flowchart** is a diagram of the steps of a solution using standard symbols joined by arrows.

- **Oval (terminator)**: Start / Stop.
- **Parallelogram**: Input / Output.
- **Rectangle**: process (calculation, assignment).
- **Diamond**: decision, one entry, two exits (Yes/No or True/False).
- **Arrows**: flow direction. **Circle**: connector.

Rules: one Start, at least one Stop; flow top to bottom, left to right; every decision branch must rejoin or end; no crossing lines.

Three structures: **sequence**, **selection** (diamond), **loop** (arrow back to a diamond).
subtopics.basics_md: A flowchart is a road map. Boxes are places, arrows are roads, and a diamond is a fork where you must choose a road.
key_points: Oval Start/Stop, parallelogram I/O, rectangle process, diamond decision
Arrows show the flow; connector joins distant parts
Decision has two exits labelled Yes/No
Three structures: sequence, selection, loop

subtopics.title: Flowcharts with decisions
subtopics.theory_md:
Turn each rule of the problem into a diamond. For **nested** conditions, test the largest-first or smallest-first ranges in order (`budget <= 100000`, then `<= 200000`, else the rest) so each range is checked once.

For a **percentage** rule, compute `spent = percent/100 * budget` in a rectangle after the decision. For an "extra weight" rule, find the excess first, then `amount = extra * rate`, and GST as `amount * 0.18`.

Every branch ends at one common Output, then Stop. Always write the **pseudocode** when the paper asks for it: IF / ELSE IF / ELSE / END IF.

subtopics.title: Flowcharts with loops and counters
subtopics.theory_md:
A **loop** is a decision whose No-exit goes on and Yes-exit loops back through an update box. Four parts: **initialise**, **test**, **body**, **update**.

- Counter: `count = count + 1` for each event.
- Fixed repeat (100 students): `i = 1`, test `i <= 100`, `i = i + 1`.
- Series: keep the previous two terms, `c = 2*b + a`, then `a = b`, `b = c`.

In a repeat-until-no loop (more complaints? y/n) the test comes at the end. Initialise counters **before** the loop, display totals **after** it (or inside, if asked after every entry).
subtopics.basics_md: A loop is a lap counter on a racetrack: start at zero, check if the laps are finished, run one more lap, add one, check again.
key_points: Initialise counters before the loop
Test, body, update; arrow back to the test
Fixed repeat uses i = 1, i <= n, i = i + 1
Totals displayed after the loop unless asked each time

subtopics.title: What an algorithm is and how to write one
subtopics.theory_md:
An **algorithm** is a finite, step-by-step procedure to solve a problem.

**Properties**: finite, definite (each step clear), input (zero or more), output (one or more), effective (each step doable).

Write it as: **Start**, declare/**Input**, numbered steps with `If ... then ... else`, **Output**, **Stop**. **Pseudocode** is the same in code-like English. Use `mod` for remainder: `n mod 2 = 0` means even.

Algorithm = steps in words; flowchart = steps as a diagram; program = steps in a language.
subtopics.basics_md: An algorithm is a recipe: precise steps, in order, that end with the dish ready.
key_points: Finite, definite, input, output, effective
Start, input, steps, output, Stop
Even test: n mod 2 = 0
Algorithm in words, flowchart as diagram, program in code

**Difference:** an algorithm is written in words as numbered steps; a flowchart is the graphical form using symbols and arrows.

subtopics.title: Algorithms with conditions
subtopics.theory_md:
Convert each sentence of the problem into an **If**. Use **AND** when all factors must hold, **OR** when any one suffices, and **nested If** or **Else If** when only one outcome is allowed.

- Independent messages (placement, society) are **separate If** blocks, so more than one can print.
- Mutually exclusive choices (aeroplane or train) use If/Else.
- A repeated check (wrong password) uses a **While** loop until correct.

Name the variables and their type first, then list steps. End with an example input and output.
subtopics.basics_md: Read the paper like a rulebook: each sentence is an if-then. Say which rules can fire together and which exclude each other.

subtopics.title: Algorithms with loops and counters
subtopics.theory_md:
For "100 students" use **For i = 1 to 100**. Set the counters (`male_count = 0`) **before** the loop, update inside, display after.

Steps: **initialise, loop, input per item, test, count**.

- Range test: `age >= 18 AND age <= 25` (both inclusive).
- Not eligible if any one criterion fails: `weight < 45 OR age < 18 OR ...`; start with `eligible = TRUE` and set FALSE.
- Gender-based limits: male 90 days, female 120 days.
- Tie break: higher votes win; if equal, compare JEE marks.

Check: `male + female + not_eligible = 100`.
